about: Plain-English definitions. These are words, not measurements, so unlike everything else in site/data/ this file is written by hand rather than generated. Keep every definition to one or two sentences a non-programmer could read out loud.

story point.short: A team's own unit for how much work a task is.
story point.more: Teams pick from a fixed set — 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 — a bit like choosing a T-shirt size. The numbers mean nothing outside the team that chose them: one team's 8 can be another team's 3.

issue.short: One task in a project's tracker: a bug, a feature, a chore.
issue.more: It has a title, usually a description, a type and a priority. That text is all this project's model gets to look at.

federated learning.short: Training one shared model without collecting the data in one place.
federated learning.more: Each participant trains on its own data and sends only what it learned — never the data itself. A server averages those contributions and sends the result back.

client.short: One participant in federated training. Here, one software project.
client.more: Eighteen projects take part. Each keeps its own issues and only ever uploads a small bundle of trained numbers.

round.short: One turn of federated training: everyone trains, the server merges.
round.more: The run on this site used sixty rounds. A round is not the same as an epoch — inside one round, each project does its own local training.

epoch.short: One pass through a set of training examples.
epoch.more: If a project has 1,000 issues, one epoch means the model has seen all thousand once.

encoder.short: The part that turns words into numbers.
encoder.more: It reads the issue text and produces a long list of numbers standing for its meaning. Everything after it works on those numbers, never on the words.

codebert.short: The particular encoder this project uses.
codebert.more: A model trained on both English and source code, which suits issue text full of class names and stack traces.

token.short: A chunk of text — roughly a word or part of one.
token.more: Models read tokens, not letters. A long issue has to be cut off at some limit, which is why very long issues lose their endings.

head.short: The small final part that turns the numbers into an answer.
head.more: The encoder understands the text; the head decides which story point that means. In the personalised setup, each project keeps its own head.

lora.short: A way to adjust a big model by training a small patch instead of all of it.
lora.more: The original model is left frozen, and a small pair of matrices is trained alongside it. That patch is a fraction of a percent of the model's size, which is what makes sending it around practical.

adapter.short: Another word for the small trained patch.
adapter.more: It sits alongside a frozen model and nudges its behaviour, without the model itself being changed.

ffa-lora.short: LoRA with one half of the patch frozen, so that merging is exact.
ffa-lora.more: A patch is two matrices multiplied together. Averaging them separately does not give the average of the products. Freezing one half — everyone shares the same one — makes the difference exactly zero.

fedavg.short: The plain way to merge: average what every participant sends.
fedavg.more: Each project's contribution is weighted by how much data it trained on.

fedprox.short: FedAvg plus a pull back towards the shared model.
fedprox.more: Projects with very different data drift apart during their local training. A tension term holds each one loosely to the group, so the merge stays useful.

personalised head.short: Each project keeps its own final layer instead of sharing it.
personalised head.more: The shared part learns what a complicated issue looks like; the private part learns what this particular team calls an 8.

warm start.short: Training on one large project first, to give everyone a sensible starting point.
warm start.more: It is also the one place in this design where data is pooled, which the site says plainly rather than glossing over.

training set.short: The issues the model learns from.
training set.more: Here it is about 23,000 issues, kept separate from everything used to judge the model.

check set.short: Issues held back to choose between versions of the model.
check set.more: Usually called the validation set. Using it to pick the best round is fine; using the test set for that would be cheating.

test set.short: Issues held back to the very end, to measure the model once.
test set.more: Around 6,400 issues. Looking at them more than once turns a measurement into a decision, and the number stops meaning anything.

ordinal.short: Ordered categories: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 have an order, but not fixed spacing.
ordinal.more: This is why guessing 8 when the answer is 3 should count as a worse mistake than guessing 2 — even though both are simply 'wrong'.

corn.short: A way of predicting ordered answers by asking a chain of yes/no questions.
corn.more: Is it bigger than 1? Bigger than 2? Bigger than 3? A distant miss gets more of those questions wrong, so being far out costs more than being close.

macro-f1.short: How well the model does on every class, counting rare ones as much as common ones.
macro-f1.more: It says nothing about how near a miss was: predicting 8 for a 3 is penalised exactly like predicting 2.

mae.short: Mean absolute error: on average, how far off the guess is.
mae.more: In story points. An error of 1.2 means the typical guess is a little over one step away from the truth.

kappa.short: A score that asks whether you did better than lucky guessing.
kappa.more: Zero means no better than chance. The weighted version used here also counts how far off each mistake was.

confusion matrix.short: A grid of what was guessed against what was true.
confusion matrix.more: Its shape matters more than its total: mistakes clustered next to the diagonal mean the model has the right idea and the wrong step.

baseline.short: A deliberately simple method, there to make a result mean something.
baseline.more: 'Our model scores 0.25' says nothing until you know what always guessing the middle value scores.

tf-idf.short: An old, simple way of turning text into numbers by counting words.
tf-idf.more: It weighs a word by how often it appears here against how rare it is everywhere. No understanding of meaning at all — which is what makes it such a useful comparison.

svm.short: A classic, small machine-learning method that draws dividing lines between classes.
svm.more: Paired with word counts it is the standard 'simple model' comparison in this field.

seed.short: The number that fixes all the random choices, so a run can be repeated.
seed.more: Same seed, same shuffles, same starting values, same result.

overfitting.short: Learning the training examples rather than the pattern behind them.
overfitting.more: It looks like improvement on data the model has seen and gets worse on anything new.

non-iid.short: Participants whose data does not look alike.
non-iid.more: Some projects here mostly use 1s and 2s; others spread across the whole range. That unevenness is the central difficulty this design has to cope with.

pooling.short: Throwing every project's results into one pile and scoring that.
pooling.more: It can flatter a model badly: a predictor that only knows which project a row came from scores well pooled and nothing at all per project.
